We Are Your Local Milwaukee Market Experts!


Milwaukee’s homes are notably old. About 34.67% of homes were built before 1939, and another 16.48% were built between 1970 and 1999. Only about 7.52% of the housing stock was built in 2000 or later. This makes Milwaukee one of the older housing markets in the Midwest, with the majority of homes dating from the early-to-mid 20th century.

Common Problems in Milwaukee Homes
Given the age of the housing stock, buyers and renters should be aware of several recurring issues:

Lead paint: Lead-based paint is present in at least 100,000 Milwaukee homes. Older homes, typically those built before 1978, may contain deteriorated lead-based paint or friable asbestos that require qualified remediation.
Lead pipes: Some residents are also concerned about lead pipes in the water supply, though the water is treated to reduce lead levels.
Asbestos: Homes built before the 1970s often contain asbestos in insulation, flooring, and roofing materials, which can cause serious lung disease if disturbed.
Outdated electrical and plumbing: Most houses built in the early 20th century were not wired for the number of electronics, lights, and appliances common today. Older homes may also have lead plumbing that requires filtration or full replumbing.
Water infiltration and foundation issues: Inspectors frequently flag cracked or missing siding, rotted trim, failed caulking, poor grading, and hardscape issues that direct water toward foundations — all common in aging Milwaukee homes.
Chimney and roof deterioration: Cracked flue liners, loose crown mortar, and missing chimney caps are frequently cited defects, along with window and door failures involving rot and broken seals.

Here’s a few answers to common ones.

Who Are We?

Our company is a real estate investment firm, and we focus on helping home owners who need to sell their homes fast do that. With no hassle.

What’s It Cost To Work With Us?

Nothing. There are no fees or commissions. We don’t list your home… we’re looking to actually buy your home ourselves. Plus, we even pay for all of the closing costs and other costs associated with the sale. Can’t beat that right? 🙂

Frequently Asked Questions

Maybe you have a few questions. That’s okay; most people do. So here’s a quick collection of some of the questions people ask us… along with our answers. If you still have a question, don’t hesitate to contact us (or give us a call) and we’ll be happy to answer it for you.

Q:  Will you be listing my house on the MLS or actually buying it?
A:  Great question. We’re not agents, and we don’t list houses. We are professional home buyers: We buy houses in Milwaukee that meet our purchasing criteria. From there we may repair the house and resell it to another homeowner or keep it as a rental ourselves.

Q:  Do you pay fair prices for properties?
A:  Many of the houses we purchase are below market value (we do this so we can resell it at a profit to another homeowner). We are looking to get a fair discount on a property. However, in our experience, many sellers aren’t necessarily expecting a large “windfall” on the property but rather appreciate that we can offer cash, we close very quickly (no waiting for financing), and no time, effort, or expense is required on your part of fix up the property or pay agent fees. Q:  How do you determine the price to offer on my house?
A:  Great question, and we’re an open book: Our process is very straightforward. We look at the location of the property, what repairs are needed, the current condition of the property, and the values of comparable houses sold in the area recently. As you know, house values have taken a huge hit in the last 5 years and most areas still haven’t seen prices come back up. We take many pieces of information into consideration… and come up with a fair price that works for us and works for you too.

Q:  Are there any fees or commissions to work with you?
A: This is what makes us stand out from the traditional method of selling your house: There are NO fees or commissions when you sell your house to us. We’ll make you an offer, and if it’s a fit then we’ll buy your house (and we’ll often pay for the closing costs too!). No hassle. No fees. Q:  How are you different from a real estate agent?
A: Real estate agents list properties and hope that someone will buy them. The agent shows the properties to prospective buyers if there are any (the average time to sell a property in many markets right now is 6-12 months) and then takes a percentage of the sale price if they find a buyer. Oftentimes, the agent’s commission is 3-6% of the sale price of your house (so if it’s a $100,000 house, you’ll pay between $3,000 – $6,000 in commissions to an agent). Agents provide a great service for those who can wait 6-12 months to sell and who don’t mind giving up some of that sale price to pay for the commissions. But that’s where we’re different: We’re not agents, we’re home buyers. Our company actually buys houses. We don’t list houses. Again, we make our living by taking the risk to buy the house with our own cash, repair the house, and market it ourselves to find a buyer (which is the hard part in this market).

Q:  Is there any obligation when I submit my info?
A: There is absolutely zero obligation for you. Once you tell us a bit about your property, we’ll take a look at things, maybe set up a call with you to find out a bit more, and make you an all-cash offer that’s fair for you and fair for us. “I Need To Sell My House Fast In The Waukesha!”

We Buy Houses With Cash Anywhere In The Waukesha And Other Parts of Wisconsin, And At Any Price. Check Out How Our Process Works. We’re Ready To Give You All Cash For Your House.

Waukesha, Wisconsin is a county-seat city of about 71,000 west of Milwaukee, with a housing stock that spans nearly its whole history rather than clustering in one era. It was settled in 1834, became known as “Spring City” for its mineral springs and enjoyed a health-resort boom into the early 1900s, then shifted to manufacturing with the founding of the Waukesha Motor Company in 1906. Post-WWII suburbanization added a large wave of single-family homes, and the city has kept growing modestly since (roughly 64,800 in 2000 to about 71,000 today). The result is a genuinely layered housing stock: the downtown/historic core dates to the late 1800s and early 1900s, the Fox River corridor is largely 1920s-60s, and areas like Sunset Heights and East Waukesha are mostly 1950s-80s mid-century construction, with newer subdivisions concentrated in South Waukesha.

Common housing issues in Waukesha:

  • Radium-contaminated groundwater — this is a well-documented, area-specific issue: Waukesha’s deep sandstone aquifer wells had radium levels exceeding drinking-water standards, which forced the city to build an entirely new water supply pipeline from Lake Michigan (via Milwaukee Water Works), completed around 2023. Homes still on older private or shallow wells in the surrounding area can be more exposed to this kind of groundwater quality issue.
  • Aging electrical systems in the historic core — homes from the late 1800s-1950s (downtown, Fox River corridor, Carroll University district) commonly have knob-and-tube wiring with brittle, deteriorating insulation, while homes from the 1960s-70s often have aluminum wiring prone to loose connections and inadequate grounding.
  • Undersized electrical panels — many older homes still run 60- or 100-amp service, insufficient for modern appliance and HVAC loads.
  • Aging heating systems — older housing stock in this climate often relies on boilers and radiators or furnaces well past typical service life.
  • Lead-based paint — a real consideration in the pre-1978 housing stock, especially the 19th- and early-20th-century downtown core.
  • Foundation and basement moisture issues — Wisconsin’s freeze-thaw cycles commonly stress older masonry foundations and basements lacking modern waterproofing, particularly in the Fox River corridor and Sunset Heights/East Waukesha homes.
  • Inefficient windows and insulation — original single-pane windows and minimal insulation are common in pre-1980 homes, contributing to drafts and winter ice damming.
  • Possible asbestos-containing materials — a consideration in renovation or demolition work on the city’s older (pre-1980s) housing.

content:
“I Need To Sell My House Fast In The Racine!”

We Buy Houses With Cash Anywhere In The Racine And Other Parts of Wisconsin, And At Any Price. Check Out How Our Process Works. We’re Ready To Give You All Cash For Your House.

Racine, Wisconsin has one of the oldest housing stocks in the region — the city’s own 2025 housing study puts the median dwelling age at nearly 60 years, with only about 13.4% of homes built since 1980. That age profile drives most of the issues buyers and owners run into.

Common issues in Racine’s housing stock:

  • Lead water service lines — this is a live, documented issue: the city is in the middle of a $130 million project to replace roughly 10,000 lead service lines (the underground pipes connecting individual homes to the water main), work that began in May 2026 and is slated to run over five years. Lead lines were standard practice for decades and are common in a city this old.
  • Lead-based paint — with the bulk of the housing stock predating 1980, and a historic core dating to the 1840s-1920s, lead paint in older layers of interior and exterior paint is a routine hazard in homes that haven’t been remediated.
  • Outdated electrical systems — homes built before 1950 (common in Racine’s older neighborhoods) frequently still have knob-and-tube wiring, where the original rubber insulation has become brittle and flakes off, exposing bare wire; homes from the 1960s-70s often have aluminum wiring instead, which loosens at outlets and switches from thermal expansion and lacks a dedicated ground. Many older homes also still run on undersized 60- or 100-amp electrical panels inadequate for modern appliance loads.
  • Aging heating systems — older Midwestern housing stock of this era commonly used boilers and radiators rather than forced-air furnaces; both boiler and furnace equipment installed decades ago is now well past typical service life in a lot of Racine homes.

title: Selling an Inherited Property in Wisconsin | Kustom Property Solutions
heading: Selling an Inherited Property in Wisconsin
description: If you’ve recently inherited a home or other property and are considering selling it, we’re here to help. Reach out to us to receive a competitive cash offer!
content:
Inheriting a home or property often brings a mix of emotions, along with unexpected financial responsibilities. You might be wondering if major repairs or costly upgrades are needed, how much tax you’ll owe, or if the property must go through probate due to the absence of a will. While these factors can feel overwhelming, inherited properties also offer a unique opportunity for buyers and investors seeking a discounted home to personalize. So, what’s involved in selling a property you’ve inherited? Are there specific steps required to manage this type of sale? This guide walks you through the process of preparing and selling an inherited property to help you turn it into a profitable venture.

How To Sell An Inherited Property in Wisconsin

Inheriting a property often leads to questions about what steps come next. In most cases, the property must undergo a probate process, which allows the courts to legally confirm the rightful owner. Probate is essentially a legal procedure where the Court facilitates the transfer of the estate’s assets, such as property, to the designated heirs or beneficiaries. The duration of probate can vary significantly—sometimes it’s a straightforward process, but other times, depending on the will’s condition (if one exists), it can be prolonged.

Identifying the Estate Executor

When a will accompanies an inherited property, identifying the estate executor is usually straightforward. A crucial role of a will is to appoint an executor who can legally manage and distribute the deceased’s assets as directed. Before any assets listed in the will, including real estate, can be sold, the will must be validated through probate court. Once the court approves, the executor has the authority to fulfill the deceased’s instructions regarding asset distribution. However, if the will is contested or absent, the process can become lengthier, as additional legal intervention is required.

In cases without a designated executor, the probate court assigns an impartial administrator to handle the estate’s responsibilities. Similar to an executor, the administrator’s role includes managing any estate debts, distributing assets to heirs, and determining if any property must be sold to settle debts, such as outstanding taxes or mortgages. This appointed administrator ensures that the deceased’s intentions are honored, even when family members are not directly involved in the process.

Navigating Probate with Legal and Real Estate Experts

The probate process can be complex and challenging, which is why having a skilled attorney by your side is invaluable when selling an inherited property. A knowledgeable lawyer can help you avoid common legal pitfalls and guide you through each probate requirement. Once you have the green light from the probate court to proceed with the sale, partnering with a real estate agent experienced in handling inherited properties is your next essential step.

A real estate agent well-versed in probate sales knows the specific legalities and nuances involved in selling inherited homes. They can connect you with the right buyer to maximize your return and offer insights on what upgrades or repairs are worth pursuing. By advising on which improvements will attract buyers and which could be skipped, they can help you avoid unnecessary costs. Their guidance can be crucial in ensuring the property sells quickly and at the best possible price, preventing the house from lingering on the market or selling below its value.

Handling Outstanding Debts

When you think of inheritance, you might picture a valuable property gifted from a relative, but the reality is often more complex. Many inherited properties come with financial obligations—such as liens on the title, unpaid back taxes, or a mortgage—that can impact the profit potential. In many cases, managing a loved one’s estate involves addressing their outstanding debts, whether they are back taxes, home loans, or even credit card balances.

Before any proceeds from the estate can be distributed to heirs, these debts must be settled first. While an inherited house can appear to be a valuable asset, it can quickly become a financial burden if these issues aren’t addressed. Consulting with an experienced estate advisor can help you understand your options for managing the estate’s debts and determining whether selling the property or finding alternative solutions is the most beneficial path forward.

Preparing an Inherited Property for the Market

After probate clears and you officially take ownership, your next decision is whether to move in, rent it out, or sell the property. In many cases, inherited homes are left in less-than-ideal condition, needing everything from a deep clean to extensive repairs. Years of deferred maintenance, combined with outdated features, often mean the property requires significant effort to bring it up to market standards.

This stage of handling an inheritance is frequently overlooked but essential. If the property has been neglected or lacks modern updates, you may find that renovations are necessary to make it appealing to buyers or tenants. Whether it’s a thorough cleaning, minor touch-ups, or a full renovation, getting the property market-ready can increase its value and help you make the most of this inherited asset.

Contact Us today for your cash offer!

Reach out to us today for a competitive cash offer on your inherited property, whether it’s a house, condo, or land. We purchase homes in any condition and can simplify the complex probate process, ensuring a smooth and hassle-free sale. Let us help you turn your inherited property into cash without the usual challenges.

Do all heirs have to agree to sell the property?

Not necessarily. If a will or probate court has already assigned ownership of an inherited property, heirs don’t need unanimous agreement to proceed with a sale. However, if ownership hasn’t been clearly established—such as in cases where there is no will, or an administrator has been appointed by the court—then all heirs must consent to sell the property. This requirement also applies to properties auctioned by the court to cover estate debts. If a buyer wins the property at auction but some heirs dispute the sale, the transaction may be delayed until the disagreement is resolved, and a settlement is reached.

Settling Disputes Among Heirs

When heirs disagree over an inherited estate, several approaches can help resolve the issue. The first priority is to ensure that an executor is in place. An executor acts as a neutral representative, tasked with upholding the wishes outlined in the will, which can prevent conflicts over asset distribution.

If no executor was appointed, or if the will itself is under dispute, hiring a mediator is often the next best step. Bringing in a neutral third party can help facilitate productive discussions and find common ground without the high costs and delays of a full probate court proceeding. Mediation can be a cost-effective way to settle disagreements, keeping the process smoother and less contentious for everyone involved.

Handling Executor-Related Disputes

Conflicts can arise when a family member is named as the executor or trustee, as emotions and differing opinions may lead to tension. If this situation feels too challenging, the appointed executor has the option to step aside and appoint an impartial fiduciary—such as an estate-planning attorney—to oversee the estate’s administration. Bringing in a neutral professional can help reduce family friction, allowing everyone to navigate their grief without added strain. This choice not only prevents potential arguments but also preserves family relationships by giving all parties the space needed to process their emotions.

How is inherited property taxed when sold?

In 2020, state and local governments across the U.S. collected over $5.3 billion from estate and inheritance taxes. With such significant revenue involved, understanding how inherited property is taxed when sold is crucial. Tax laws for inherited assets vary widely by state, so it’s essential to research applicable regulations in your area. Consulting an estate planning attorney with expertise in inheritance and tax laws can provide valuable guidance, whether you’re handling an unexpected inheritance or preparing your own estate plan. This professional insight can help you navigate the complexities of estate taxes and ensure compliance with local requirements.

State Tax Laws

Tax laws for inherited property sales vary widely across the United States. Some states impose estate taxes, inheritance taxes, and even capital gains taxes when an inherited property is sold. Currently, twelve states require an estate tax, five levy an inheritance tax, and one state applies both. These taxes can significantly impact the final proceeds from an inherited property sale, so it’s essential to understand the specific tax obligations in your state. Consulting a tax professional or estate attorney familiar with local inheritance and property tax laws can help you navigate these requirements and optimize your financial outcome.

Capital Gains Tax on Inherited Property

Capital gains tax applies to the profit made when an inherited asset, such as a property, is sold for more than its original value. This tax is only triggered upon sale, not at the time of inheritance. The taxable amount is based on the difference between the property’s sale price and its stepped-up basis (the fair market value at the time of the decedent’s death).

While most states impose capital gains tax on profits from inherited property sales, some offer exemptions. For instance, in Washington State, properties sold for under $250,000 are exempt from capital gains tax. Additionally, options such as reinvesting the proceeds into another property or using tax deferment strategies may help reduce the tax burden.

For guidance tailored to your circumstances, consult a tax attorney familiar with local real estate laws to explore potential exemptions or strategies before selling.

Estate Taxes

Estate tax is levied directly on the estate before assets are distributed to heirs. While the thought of a hefty tax can be intimidating, there’s often no need for concern due to the high federal exemption threshold. In 2023, estates valued under $12.92 million for individuals are exempt from this tax, meaning only estates surpassing this value will face federal estate tax on the portion above $12,920,000.

Interestingly, as this exemption threshold rises, some states have been phasing out estate taxes altogether, opting to forgo millions in potential revenue. However, estate tax laws vary by state, so consulting with a knowledgeable estate planner or tax professional can clarify any applicable state requirements before inheritance distributions are made.

Do You Need to Pay Inheritance Taxes?

Inheritance tax is only applied in six U.S. states—Maryland, Nebraska, Kentucky, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Iowa—so most heirs are exempt. If you live in one of these states, you may be required to pay taxes on the assets or properties you inherit. However, inheritance tax is based on the deceased’s residence, not the heir’s. So, if the decedent lived in one of the 44 states without an inheritance tax, you won’t owe any tax on your inheritance, regardless of where you reside.

For heirs in inheritance tax states, consulting with a tax advisor familiar with local laws can clarify your responsibilities and help you navigate potential tax obligations.

heading: Can I Sell My Home If It’s In Foreclosure in Wisconsin?
description: With a cash buyer, you can skip the lengthy process of foreclosure, eviction, and auction within a matter of days, and save your credit as well!
content:
Can I Sell My Home if its in foreclosure in Wisconsin? Foreclosure occurs when a homeowner can no longer keep up with mortgage payments and cannot catch up on missed amounts. Since a mortgage is a formal contract between you and your lender, once you default, the lender has the right to sell the property to recover what you owe. This leaves homeowners vulnerable to eviction and significant credit damage.

No one wants to receive a foreclosure notice, yet a nationwide study found that close to one million Americans worried about losing their homes (U.S. Census Bureau Household Pulse Survey, July 27–August 8, 2022). Foreclosure can develop from all sorts of life changes, such as:

  • Job loss or reduced income
  • Divorce or death of a spouse
  • Mounting debt from credit cards or medical bills
  • Relocating before managing to sell the home
  • Destruction from natural disasters

Kustom Property Solutions, a local business based in Wisconsin, has built its services around helping homeowners with distressed properties. They buy houses with cash and can often speed up what would otherwise be a drawn-out selling process, avoiding extra fees or uncertainty tied to traditional real estate methods.

What is Foreclosure?

Foreclosure is a legal course of action your lender initiates when mortgage payments remain overdue for too long. Suppose you or your spouse loses a job. The bills still pile up, but the money to cover them simply isn’t there. Even if you find work later, the accumulated debt may be too large to pay off quickly, prompting the bank to begin foreclosure. In the final stages, the property can be auctioned, leaving you without a home and a severely impacted credit score.

How Long Do You Have To Get Out of Your House After Foreclosure?

Foreclosure typically unfolds in a series of steps:

  1. Missed mortgage payments
  2. Public notice of default
  3. Formal foreclosure proceedings
  4. Auction of the home
  5. Eviction (if the homeowner remains in the property)

The exact duration for each step varies widely by state. You might have 120 days before the formal foreclosure begins, or it could stretch to nine months or more. During this period, the lender usually tries multiple times to contact you—by phone, mail, or email—to discuss your options. Should you fail to find a repayment solution, the lender will set an auction date, after which you can be forced to leave.

The Different Types of Foreclosure

There are two different types of foreclosure you may experience: nonjudicial foreclosure or judicial foreclosure.

What Is Non-Judicial Foreclosure? 

Non-judicial foreclosure does not involve taking the homeowner to court. Relying on a “power-of-sale” clause in the deed of trust, the lender can reclaim and sell your Wisconsin property when mortgage defaults continue. Because non-judicial foreclosure avoids legal battles in court, lenders often favor it for being faster and less costly, as long as state law permits it.

What Is Judicial Foreclosure?

By contrast, judicial foreclosure requires the lender to file a lawsuit, formally requesting approval from a judge to foreclose on the home. Once notified of this lawsuit, you have a chance to respond. If you lose or do not reply, the lender wins by default, and the property goes up for a foreclosure sale. If the sale price doesn’t cover your outstanding mortgage, you remain liable for the gap—this shortfall is called a deficiency judgment. Given the expenses and time involved, many lenders see judicial foreclosure as a last resort, yet it remains compulsory in some states where non-judicial foreclosure isn’t allowed.

Get an offer today, sell in a matter of days.

How to Sell Your House Before Foreclosure in Wisconsin

The period before foreclosure concludes is critical. Selling your home swiftly can help you repay your debt and potentially save your credit. Below are some of the most popular ways to do so:

Hire A Real Estate Agent

Most people consider hiring a local real estate agent first. Agents can post your home on the Multiple Listing Service (MLS), manage showings, and provide advice on pricing or staging. This may work well in a conventional setting, but if foreclosure is near, time might not be on your side. A traditional home sale can take weeks to find a buyer—and another month or longer to close—stretching well beyond the schedule you have. Plus, you’ll pay an agent’s commission of roughly 3% to 6% once the sale finalizes, further reducing how much money goes toward your mortgage debt.

Short Sale

If you owe more on your mortgage than your property is worth, you may need a short sale. A short sale requires lender approval to sell the home for less than the total mortgage balance. For instance, if you owe $250,000 but the home can only command $200,000 in the current market, a short sale could be an option. To get the lender’s green light, you must demonstrate financial hardship, typically through documentation like W-2s, medical bills, or proof of long-term unemployment.

Banks often favor short sales over foreclosures because they can still recoup some of their costs without a lengthy legal process. However, a short sale also stays on your credit report, which can make it difficult to obtain future loans or credit cards for years, similar to a foreclosure mark. Additionally, you’ll still be dealing with realtor fees or legal costs for the transaction itself.

Sell Your House AS-IS to A Cash Buyer

When time is tight, selling your home “as-is” to a reliable cash buyer can be the quickest avenue. Cash buyers purchase the property in its current condition—no need to schedule repairs, repaint rooms, or stage the house. Key benefits of selling directly to a cash investor include:

  • A closing process that may wrap up in as little as a week
  • Zero commissions or fees paid to real estate agents
  • No open houses or repeated showings
  • No uncertainty tied to a buyer’s loan approval

For homeowners at risk of immediate foreclosure, this speed can make all the difference. Although the cash offer may be somewhat lower than a conventional listing might achieve, you stand to save thousands by bypassing agent commissions, appraisal fees, and possible repairs. More importantly, a rapid sale might let you pay off your lender before the auction date, sparing you the devastating aftermath of foreclosure.

Can You Stop Foreclosure Once it Starts?

Even if the process has begun, there may still be opportunities to halt or at least delay foreclosure proceedings. Consider the following methods:

Pay Off Your Loan & Fees

The most direct solution is to become current on your mortgage. This means paying all missed payments, plus late fees and any related legal expenses. If relatives can help or you have other assets you can sell, raising those funds quickly might resolve the issue before the house goes to auction. Sometimes, lenders will arrange a repayment plan or consider modifying the existing mortgage if they see you are committed to catching up. However, the longer you wait, the fewer options remain.

Declare Bankruptcy 

Another option is bankruptcy, which imposes an “automatic stay” that generally pauses foreclosure activities. Yet bankruptcy carries significant downsides. The filing appears on your credit for up to seven years, raising your future borrowing costs and restricting your access to credit cards or loans. There’s also the legal expense and time investment needed to work with a bankruptcy attorney. While declaring bankruptcy can give you a bit more time to figure things out, it is typically a last resort because of its long-term impact on your financial standing.

The Homeowner Affordability and Stability Plan (HASP) 

If your current mortgage payment is beyond your ability to pay due to lost income or other financial struggles, the Homeowner Affordability & Stability Plan (HASP) might provide help. This government program allows eligible homeowners to modify their loan terms to reduce monthly obligations. By extending the loan length, lowering the interest rate, or otherwise adjusting the structure, HASP makes payments more manageable. To apply, you’ll need proof of consistent income (even if lower than before) and evidence that you cannot afford the original monthly payment. While not everyone qualifies, it could be a viable path to preserving your home. Apply for the program here to see if you qualify.

  • Fast closings: Traditional sales can take a month or more to conclude, while cash transactions may wrap up in mere days if needed.
  • No repairs required: Investors who buy as-is seldom require you to fix leaks, address wear and tear, or remodel outdated kitchens and bathrooms.
  • Fewer fees: With no realtor commissions and minimal closing costs, more of the sale price goes toward settling what you owe.
  • Reduced uncertainty: Mortgage applications can fall through, but cash purchases don’t rely on bank approvals.

You might not get the absolute highest price your home could fetch in a strong seller’s market, yet the speed and simplicity often tip the scales in your favor. You avoid having the property sold off at a bank auction for much less, and you control the timeline, thereby shielding your credit from the devastating blow of a completed foreclosure.

You may not receive your property’s full market value when choosing a direct cash sale, but avoiding agent commissions, drawn-out escrow periods, and repair costs can help offset that difference. More importantly, because a reputable investor can close swiftly, you can often finalize everything before the lender sets a foreclosure auction date. This means you maintain control over the sale price, as opposed to watching your home sold for a fraction of its worth at auction.

Remember, if you wait too long, the bank may move forward with a sale that leaves you with limited or no options. Acting quickly to explore your choices—whether that involves catching up on payments, negotiating with your lender, applying for government-backed relief, or selling to a trusted cash buyer—can provide the best chance of a successful outcome. Ultimately, if you’re wondering, “Can I Sell My Home if its in foreclosure in Wisconsin?,” the answer is often yes. title: Selling a House with Foundation Issues | Kustom Property Solutions
heading: Selling a House With Foundation Problems in Wisconsin: What You Need to Know
description: If have a home with foundation issues and are considering selling it, we’re here to help. Reach out to us to receive a competitive cash offer!
content:
Foundation issues are one of the most stressful discoveries a homeowner can face — especially when you’re trying to sell. The good news? Kustom Property Solutions is your local expert. Whether your home has a wet basement, minor hairline cracks or more serious structural concerns, selling quickly is absolutely possible. Here’s what you need to know.

Why Wisconsin Homes Are Especially Vulnerable

Wisconsin’s freeze-thaw cycle is brutal on foundations. Every winter, moisture in the soil surrounding your home freezes, expands, and shifts — then thaws and contracts again in spring. Over years and decades, this repeated movement puts enormous pressure on concrete and block foundations. Add in clay-heavy soils common across much of the state, and you have a recipe for cracking, bowing, and settling.

This isn’t a reflection of how well you’ve maintained your home. It’s geology and climate doing what they do. But it does mean foundation issues are remarkably common in Wisconsin — and buyers and their agents know it.

Common Foundation Problems in Wisconsin Homes

If you have a wet basement – its a warning sign. Before you decide how to proceed, it helps to understand what you’re dealing with. Not all foundation problems are created equal.

Minor issues include small vertical hairline cracks in poured concrete walls (common and often cosmetic), minor efflorescence (white mineral deposits from water seepage), and slight settling that hasn’t affected the structure.

Moderate issues include horizontal cracks in block or poured walls (a more serious warning sign), stair-step cracking in block foundations, bowing or leaning walls, and water intrusion that has caused ongoing moisture problems.

Major issues include significant structural shifting, large sections of wall failure, compromised load-bearing elements, and problems that have caused visible effects throughout the home — sloping floors, sticking doors, gaps around windows.

Wisconsin Disclosure Laws: What You’re Required to Tell Buyers

Wisconsin has some of the most comprehensive real estate disclosure requirements in the country. Under Wisconsin law (Wis. Stat. § 709.02), sellers of residential property must complete a Real Estate Condition Report (RECR) disclosing known defects — and foundation problems fall squarely within that obligation.

You must disclose:

Any known structural or foundation problems

Any history of water intrusion in the basement or crawl space (wet basement)

Any repairs that have been made to the foundation

Any drainage or grading issues that have affected the home

Failing to disclose known defects can expose you to significant legal liability, including lawsuits for misrepresentation or fraud after closing. Wisconsin courts take this seriously. Disclosure isn’t just the ethical choice — it’s the legally required one.

The practical upside: full, proactive disclosure actually makes transactions go more smoothly. Buyers who find out about issues through their own inspection after being misled are far more likely to walk away or pursue legal action. Buyers who know upfront can price and plan accordingly.

Ready to move on from Foundation Issues? Contact Us today for your cash offer!

Reach out to us today for a competitive cash offer on your house. We purchase homes in any condition and can simplify the process, ensuring a smooth and hassle-free sale. Let us help you turn your property into cash without the usual challenges.

Your Options for Selling

Once you know what you’re working with, you have a few basic paths forward.

Option 1: Repair Before Listing

If your foundation issues are moderate and the repair costs are manageable, spending the time and money to fix the problem before listing is an option. You can price the home at or near full market value and attract the pool of buyers using conventional financing, which requires the home to be in sound structural condition.

Foundation repair costs in Wisconsin vary widely: a full wall stabilization or underpinning can reach $10,000–$30,000 or more. Weigh the repair cost against your expected sale price and time on market.

Option 2: Sell to a Cash Buyer or Investor

A growing segment of the Wisconsin real estate market consists of cash buyers — like Kustom Property Solutions— who specifically seek out properties with problems. These buyers are experienced with foundation issues, won’t require a traditional mortgage appraisal, and typically move fast (sometimes closing in two to three weeks). If speed, certainty, and avoiding repair hassles are priorities, this can be the right path.

How Foundation Issues Affect Financing

This is a critical piece many sellers overlook. If your home has significant foundation problems, certain types of financing may not be available to your buyers.

FHA and VA loans have strict property condition requirements. A home with visible structural defects will typically fail the required appraisal, meaning buyers using these loan types may be unable to purchase your home without repairs first.

Conventional loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac also require properties to meet minimum condition standards. Severe foundation issues can result in an appraisal condition that must be resolved before the loan can close.

Cash buyers have no such restrictions. If you’re selling as-is, selling to buyers who don’t need conventional financing will be your fastest path closing and receiving payment.

The Bottom Line

Foundation issues are a problem to be solved — not a secret to be kept. Sellers who approach the process with transparency and a clear strategy consistently get better outcomes than those who hope no one will notice. Selling a Wisconsin home with foundation problems quickly is possible – and easy when you work with the right local team.

If you’re not sure where to start, a conversation with Kustom Property Solutions will give you a solid foundation — in every sense — for whatever comes next.

By Rizwan Ahmad

Selling a house can be a complex process that requires a lot of attention to detail. One of the things you need to pay attention to when you’re selling your house is real estate disclosures. These disclosures are designed to protect buyers and ensure that they have all the information they need to make an informed decision about purchasing your property. In this blog post, we’ll go over what you need to know about real estate disclosures when selling your house in Milwaukee.

What are real estate disclosures?

Real estate disclosures serve as a crucial tool for buyers to understand the potential risks and liabilities associated with the property they intend to purchase. These documents provide a comprehensive overview of the property’s condition, alerting buyers to any potential issues that may impact their decision. For instance, the disclosure may indicate whether the property has any structural defects, pest infestations, electrical or plumbing issues, or any other hazards. It may also specify whether the property has had any recent repairs or renovations, and whether they were performed by licensed professionals. By disclosing all relevant information, real estate disclosures help buyers make informed decisions about whether to proceed with a purchase, negotiate the terms of the sale, or even back out of the deal altogether if necessary.

Why are real estate disclosures important?

In addition to protecting buyers from unexpected surprises, real estate disclosures also help to promote transparency and honesty in the real estate industry. It is the responsibility of the seller to disclose any known issues with the property, such as water damage, mold, or structural problems. By doing so, the seller is being upfront and honest with potential buyers, which can help to build trust between the parties involved in the transaction.

Furthermore, real estate disclosures can also help to prevent legal disputes between buyers and sellers. If a seller fails to disclose a known issue with the property and the buyer discovers it after the sale, the buyer may be able to take legal action against the seller. However, if the seller provided full disclosure of any issues with the property, the buyer cannot claim that they were misled or deceived by the seller.

What needs to be disclosed?

When it comes to real estate disclosures, everything must be disclosed. This includes any known defects or issues with the property, any renovations or repairs that have been done, and any problems that have been encountered during ownership. Some common things that need to be disclosed include:

– Water damage or mold issues

– Structural problems

– Electrical or plumbing issues

– Roof leaks

– Pest infestations

– Environmental hazards

If you’re unsure about whether or not something needs to be disclosed, it’s always better to err on the side of caution and disclose it anyway.

What happens if you don’t disclose everything?

When selling a property, it’s crucial to disclose any issues or defects with the property to the buyer. Failure to disclose everything could result in serious consequences. If the buyer discovers a problem with the property that you didn’t disclose, they may take legal action against you. Not only could you face expensive fines, but you could also be required to buy back the property from the buyer. This can be incredibly costly and time-consuming, and could even harm your reputation as a seller. For these reasons, it’s always best to be upfront and honest about any issues with the property before completing the sale. This can help you avoid potential legal trouble and ensure that both you and the buyer are satisfied with the transaction.

This can save you time and money, and you can avoid having to disclose any potential problems with the property.

Kustom Property Solutions will make you a cash offer for your house and take care of all the paperwork and legal fees associated with the sale. This can make the process of selling your house much easier and less stressful.

Bottom Line When it Comes to Real Estate Disclosures

Real estate disclosures are an important part of selling a house. By disclosing everything upfront, you can protect yourself from potential legal issues and ensure that buyers have all the information they need to make an informed decision about purchasing your property. Milwaukee real estate investments can be a lucrative way to build your wealth and secure your financial future. However, there are times when an investment property may no longer be the right choice for you. In this blog post, we’ll discuss the five signs that it’s time to throw in the towel on your Milwaukee real estate investment.

1. Negative Cash Flow

Negative cash flow is a clear indication that your investment property is not performing as well as it should. It means that the expenses associated with the property, such as mortgage payments, taxes, insurance, repairs and maintenance costs, are greater than the income it generates. Negative cash flow can be a sign that it’s time to sell the property and move on to other investments that will provide a better return on investment.

2. High Vacancy Rates

Vacancy rates are another crucial factor to consider when assessing the performance of your investment property. If you have a high vacancy rate, it means that your property is not attracting tenants, and you are losing out on rental income. A high vacancy rate can be a sign that you need to re-evaluate your rental strategy or make improvements to the property to make it more appealing to potential tenants. However, if you have tried everything and the vacancy rate remains high, it may be time to sell the property and move on.

3. Declining Property Values

Real estate values are subject to market fluctuations, and it’s not uncommon for property values to rise and fall over time. However, if you notice that property values in your area have been declining consistently, it could be a sign that it’s time to sell. A declining market can make it difficult to sell your investment property for a profit, and you may end up losing money in the long run if you hold onto the property for longer than you should. In some cases, you may be better off selling right away, as opposed to waiting around for things to get worse. 

4. Major Repairs Needed

Owning an investment property comes with a host of maintenance and repair costs. While minor repairs are a part of the regular upkeep of any property, major repairs can be a significant financial burden. If your property requires major repairs that are beyond your budget, it may be time to sell the property before the situation gets worse. Delaying necessary repairs can lead to more significant problems down the line, and it may end up costing you more when all is said and done.

5. Personal Circumstances

Finally, personal circumstances can also play a role in your decision to sell your investment property in Milwaukee. Life changes such as a job relocation, divorce, or the need for immediate cash can make it necessary to sell your property quickly. In such cases, it’s essential to weigh the pros and cons of holding onto the property versus selling it quickly to meet your financial obligations.

Owning an investment property can be a rewarding experience, but it’s essential to know when it’s time to move on. How to Sell Your House During Bankruptcy in Wisconsin

March 25, 2025

By jesseharp

 

Filing for bankruptcy can feel like a storm has blown through your finances, but it doesn’t have to wash away the equity you’ve built in your home. If you need to free up cash, stop foreclosure, or reset your budget, you can sell your house—even while your case is still open. Below you’ll learn the step-by-step process, recent market and bankruptcy data that affect Wisconsin homeowners, and why a direct cash sale to Kustom Property Solutions often delivers the cleanest, fastest exit.

 Can You Sell Your House While in Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 Bankruptcy?

Yes—courts allow home sales in both chapters as long as you follow the rules. Individual bankruptcy filings jumped 13 % year-over-year in March 2025 alone, so judges are used to approving legitimate sales that help filers move on. ABI

Reorganization. Because you’re already repaying creditors through a court-approved plan, you’ll need to show how sale proceeds will shorten or satisfy that plan. Houses with solid equity often let owners pay the plan off early.

Liquidation. The trustee may sell non-exempt assets, but if your homestead exemption covers your equity, you can petition to sell the property yourself and keep the protected portion.

Ask the Court for Permission

File a Motion to Sell Real Property that lists:

  1. The contract price and buyer (a cash buyer keeps things simple).
  2. Estimated closing costs and liens.
  3. How every dollar of net proceeds will be used.

Creditors and the trustee have a set window (usually 14 days) to object. If no objections—or if the judge overrules them—you receive a signed order authorizing the sale of your house.

Add a Bankruptcy Contingency to Your Contract

Traditional buyers often shy away from properties tagged “sale subject to bankruptcy court approval,” dragging out your timeline. A cash investor like Kustom Property Solutions writes the contingency directly into the purchase agreement, then waits for your court order—no financing delays, no inspection nit-picking.

Order an Itemized Payoff Statement

Before closing, request a payoff from your mortgage servicer and any junior lienholders. Double-check:

  • Principal balance
  • Accrued interest to the projected closing date
  • Outstanding fees (late charges, legal costs, HOA liens)

Clear numbers prevent last-minute surprises and keep your court order accurate.

What Happens to Your Equity After the Sale?

  • The trustee distributes proceeds in this order—mortgage, you (up to your state homestead exemption), then unsecured creditors pro rata.
  • Net proceeds first pay the mortgage in full, then drop into your repayment plan. Many filers use the lump sum to finish the plan months—or years—early and receive a quicker discharge.

Local Market Snapshot – Why Timing Matters in Wisconsin

What is Foreclosure?

Foreclosure is the legal process that lets your lender repossess and sell the property to recover what’s owed. Once a court (judicial states) or trustee (non-judicial states) sets the sale, you’ll typically receive a notice of sale and a date to vacate.

Market snapshot: Nationwide, lenders started foreclosure on 68,794 U.S. properties in Q1 2025—up 14 percent from the previous quarter and 2 percent year-over-year. ATTOM

Consequences:

  • Your credit report lists a foreclosure for seven years, slashing scores and adding hurdles to future loan approvals. Experian Credit Report
  • You may lose any remaining equity after fees and penalties.
  • Relocation costs come out of pocket, often on short notice.

What is Preforeclosure?

Pre-foreclosure begins after you’ve missed several mortgage payments and your lender files a Notice of Default (NOD). It’s an official warning—not an eviction notice. Federal guidelines prevent the lender from starting a formal foreclosure until you’re 120 days (about four payments) behind. Bankrate

Timeframe: Depending on state laws, pre-foreclosure can last a few months up to two years, giving many homeowners a fighting chance to catch up, refinance, modify the loan, or sell before the auction gavel falls. Bankrate

Why this stage matters:

  • Late fees and interest pile up daily.
  • You can still sell, refinance, or negotiate—options that disappear once foreclosure is final.
  • A resolved pre-foreclosure hurts your credit far less than a completed foreclosure.

    No. Bringing the loan current or selling before foreclosure typically leaves only late-payment marks, not a seven-year foreclosure entry. Experian Credit Report

Options to Avoid Foreclosure in Wisconsin

  • Reinstatement: Pay the past-due amount plus fees.

  • Deed in Lieu: Hand back the keys, avoiding auction but still damaging credit.
  • Bankruptcy: Temporarily halts the sale, yet lingers on credit for up to a decade.

What is a Short Sale?

What it is – The homeowner owes more than the home is worth and asks the lender to accept less than the remaining mortgage balance (“short” payoff).

What is a Foreclosure?

Canceled mortgage debt on a primary residence can be excluded from federal income taxes under the Mortgage Forgiveness Debt Relief Act (extended through 2025).

5 Ways the Foreclosure of Your Wisconsin House Will Impact You in the Future

March 25, 2025

By jesseharp

If you’re feeling overwhelmed by the threat of foreclosure in Wisconsin, you’re certainly not alone. Life can take unexpected turns—such as job loss, medical bills, or divorce—that make it difficult to keep up with mortgage payments. Even so, it’s important to understand that the foreclosure process often moves at a slower pace than many people assume. That means you have a window of opportunity to look for solutions and safeguard your future. Lenders typically dislike foreclosure because it’s time-consuming and expensive, so they’re sometimes open to discussing alternatives before the situation grows too severe.

Unfortunately, some homeowners wait too long, hoping the problem will go away on its own. Foreclosure doesn’t just mean losing your property—it can also wipe out years of equity, lower your credit score for an extended period, and even create job-related hurdles down the line. Below, we highlight five ways the foreclosure of your Wisconsin house can impact your life, along with concrete steps you can take to help prevent or lessen the damage.

Costly

The first consequence many homeowners face is the accumulation of late fees and penalties once they fall behind on their mortgage. These charges can quickly add up, making it harder to catch up on missed payments. If your lender initiates legal action, court costs and attorney fees are added on top, escalating your overall debt even more. Meanwhile, foreclosed homes left vacant may drop in value or become targets for vandalism, further reducing what the lender can recover.

Because foreclosure is also expensive for your lender, they might be willing to adjust your payment schedule or even offer a temporary forbearance if you reach out promptly. Acting early could enable you to work out a revised plan—perhaps extending your loan term or modifying your interest rate—to stop fees from spiraling out of control.

Lose Equity

Equity represents the difference between your home’s current market value and what you owe on your mortgage. Over years of steady payments, many homeowners build this equity as a valuable asset. Sadly, the foreclosure process can strip away that hard-earned investment. Late fees, legal expenses, and a potential forced sale at a lower price can deplete any equity you’ve saved.

If you suspect you can’t continue making payments, consider a short sale before the situation escalates. A short sale involves selling your home for less than the remaining mortgage balance, but it could allow you to recoup some portion of your equity rather than losing it all through foreclosure. While it won’t always replace the full amount you’ve built up, it’s often a better alternative than walking away empty-handed.

Future Credit

A foreclosure in Wisconsin can remain on your credit report for up to seven years, marking you as a higher risk in the eyes of lenders. This red flag can lead to denied loan applications or much higher interest rates, whether you’re applying for a car loan or a new credit card. Landlords might also review your credit before approving a lease, making it tougher to secure affordable housing.

Although it’s possible to rebuild credit over time—through consistent on-time payments and keeping your debts manageable—the process takes patience. By reaching out to your lender early or considering alternatives like a short sale, you may lessen the blow to your credit score. Even small steps, like trimming monthly expenses or seeking financial counseling, can make a meaningful difference in helping you bounce back sooner.

Future Homeownership

After enduring foreclosure, the path back to owning another home can be steep. Many government-backed loan programs impose mandatory waiting periods—often between two and seven years—before you can apply again. During this gap, you’ll likely need to prove your financial health has improved, whether by showing a stable job history, reduced debt levels, or a stronger credit score.

If you act quickly to prevent a full foreclosure—through a loan modification or short sale—you might bypass some of these harsh restrictions. Lenders tend to look more favorably on homeowners who took proactive measures, rather than those who allowed the foreclosure to proceed. Preserving even a bit of your equity or maintaining a more positive payment history could keep the door open for future homeownership opportunities at a more reasonable interest rate.

Future Employment

It’s surprising to some, but the foreclosure of your Wisconsin house can even affect your career. More and more employers now run credit checks when screening job candidates—especially for roles involving finances or sensitive data. A foreclosure might raise red flags about your reliability or money management. While it’s not an automatic rejection, it can give an edge to applicants with cleaner credit histories.

If you’re aiming for a new job or hope to advance in your current position, a recent foreclosure may cast doubt on your judgment. This is another reason to confront potential foreclosure head-on. Taking steps like consulting credit counselors or working out a revised payment plan with your lender shows you’re handling problems responsibly, which can look better to a prospective employer than ignoring your financial troubles.

Practical Strategies to Avoid Foreclosure in Wisconsin

The good news is that foreclosure isn’t always inevitable. Here are several approaches that could help you avoid the worst outcomes:

  1. Contact Your Lender Early: If you see trouble on the horizon, let your lender know as soon as possible. They may offer temporary relief or modified payment structures if you demonstrate a genuine effort to catch up.
  2. Pursue a Loan Modification: Sometimes, changing the length or interest rate of your mortgage can make payments more manageable.
  3. Consider a Short Sale: Selling the property for less than you owe might sound daunting, but it can allow you to preserve a portion of your equity and protect your credit from a full foreclosure.
  4. Seek Professional Guidance: Housing counselors, real estate agents, and attorneys can offer specialized knowledge about local laws, government assistance programs, and negotiation tactics.
  5. Reevaluate Your Budget: Cutting back on non-essentials, finding a side job, or consolidating other debts may give you the financial breathing room to stay on track with mortgage payments.

How Kustom Property Solutions Can Help

If the foreclosure of your Wisconsin house feels unavoidable, Kustom Property Solutions stands ready to discuss possible solutions. Our direct buyers understand how quickly the foreclosure timeline can move, and we aim to offer stress-free, straightforward options for homeowners. A fast sale may allow you to settle debts and avoid further damage to your credit. Even if selling directly to us isn’t the perfect match, we’ll point you toward alternative resources that could be helpful.

Foreclosure is a serious matter that can ripple through nearly every part of your life, from finances to future job prospects. The best defense is knowledge—knowing your rights, the real impact of foreclosure, and the solutions available. By addressing problems early on, you can often fend off the heaviest repercussions, whether that means preserving your credit, retaining some equity, or keeping your career path open.

If you’re worried about foreclosure in Wisconsin, don’t wait for the worst-case scenario. Call Kustom Property Solutions at (262) 432-1760 or send us a message. We’re here to help you map out a strategy that fits your financial situation and safeguards your long-term goals.

What Homeowners in Wisconsin Can Expect During the Foreclosure Process

March 25, 2025

By Rizwan Ahmad

Foreclosure process in Wisconsin can feel overwhelming, yet learning each step ahead of time gives you power. Whether you recently missed a payment or already received a notice, this guide breaks down the timeline, explains your rights, and shows how a direct cash sale could let you move forward on your terms.

1. Default: The Earliest Warning

Life happens—job loss, medical bills, or an unexpected repair can derail your budget. Most lenders allow a brief grace period, generally 10–15 days, before late fees kick in. During this stage you should:

  • Call the lender’s loss‑mitigation department quickly; many offer hardship programs.

Acting early may prevent the lender from escalating the foreclosure process in Wisconsin.

2. Notice of Default: The 90‑Day Countdown Starts

If payments remain delinquent for roughly 90 days, the trustee records a Notice of Default (NOD). The clock is now visible to the public. Important points:

  • You still live in the home.
  • You have 90 more days to pay what you owe, including penalties.
  • Each missed month adds fresh late charges, so the total grows fast.

3. Mortgage Reinstatement or Workout Plans

Many owners stop foreclosure here by paying the arrears in full—called reinstatement. Can’t raise the cash? Ask about:

  1. Forbearance: Temporary reduction or pause in payments.
  2. Loan modification: Roll past‑due amounts into a new loan with longer terms.
  3. Repayment schedule: Spread arrears over several months.

Keeping communication honest often convinces the bank you want to stay, which may pause the foreclosure process in Wisconsin long enough to catch up.

4. Notice of Sale: Only 21 Days Remain

If the NOD period expires without resolution, a Notice of Sale is posted on the property and recorded at the courthouse. Key facts:

  • Your home is slated for auction in as little as three weeks.
  • The sale date, time, and location must be listed.
  • You may stay in the home until the sale occurs, but planning a move now reduces stress later.

5. Auction Day and the REO Scenario

Auctions move fast—winning bidders must pay on the spot with cash or cashier’s check. Two outcomes follow:

  • Sold to a third party: The new owner may serve a three‑day notice to quit or negotiate “cash for keys.”
  • No third‑party buyer: The property reverts to the lender and becomes real‑estate‑owned (REO). Banks often hire an agent to list the property and will eventually ask a court to evict.

6. Know Your Rights and Protections

Even late in the game, homeowners possess important protections under federal and state law:

  • Right to reinstate up to five business days before the sale.
  • Right of redemption (limited in many states) allows repurchase after sale.
  • Servicemembers Civil Relief Act offers extra time for active‑duty military.
  • COVID‑19 forbearance programs may still apply if your hardship began earlier.

Always verify deadlines with a housing counselor or attorney familiar with the foreclosure process in Wisconsin.

7. A Faster, Simpler Exit: Sell Directly to Kustom Property Solutions

When saving the loan no longer makes sense, selling before the auction lets you protect equity and your credit score. Professional cash buyers at Kustom Property Solutions make this option simple:

  1. Request a no‑obligation visit or virtual walk‑through.
  2. Receive a transparent cash offer based on current market data plus renovation costs we shoulder—not you.
  3. Pick a closing date that fits your timeline, sometimes in as little as seven days, stopping the foreclosure process in Wisconsin dead in its tracks.

8. Why Kustom Property Solutions Works for Stressed Homeowners

  • No fees or commissions: Keep every dollar of the offer.
  • As‑is purchase: Skip repairs, cleaning, and open houses.
  • Certainty: A guaranteed closing removes fear of lender delays.
  • Local team: We live and invest in Wisconsin; your success is our reputation.

Community Help and Counseling

Facing the clock alone can be scary. Thankfully, Wisconsin offers free or low‑cost housing counselors approved by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. These experts can:

  • Negotiate forbearance or loan modifications on your behalf.
  • Explain state‑specific mediation programs that pause the foreclosure timeline while talks continue.

Dial 211 or visit your state’s housing website to locate a counselor. Their guidance often adds breathing room, giving families enough time to weigh the pros and cons of refinancing, bankruptcy, or a direct sale.

Understanding the Full Timeline at a Glance

FAQ: Quick Answers

How many missed payments trigger default? Usually two to three, but each lender differs. Check your loan agreement.

Can I sell my house after receiving a Notice of Sale? Yes, until the auction gavel falls. A cash buyer like Kustom Property Solutions can move quickly.

Stopping the Foreclosure Process: A Guide for Wisconsin Homeowners

By jesseharp

Foreclosure moves faster than most people expect, and every missed payment shortens the timeline. If you are worried about stopping the foreclosure process on your Wisconsin home, this guide walks you through proven strategies— from negotiating with your lender to selling fast for cash —so you can regain control before the bank takes over. You will learn how Wisconsin’s foreclosure laws work, which government and nonprofit programs still have funding, and why working with Kustom Property Solutions can deliver the quickest, least stressful exit when time is running out.

The Wisconsin Foreclosure Clock

Wisconsin is a judicial‐foreclosure state, meaning your lender must sue you in court. Once judgment is entered, homeowners typically have a 12-month redemption period (sometimes as short as 7 working days for abandoned properties) to repay or sell before the sheriff’s sale is confirmed.docs.legis.wisconsin.govdocs.legis.wisconsin.gov

Recent data show that Wisconsin ranked 37th in foreclosure activity in late 2024, with one filing for every 8,907 housing units— 307 properties statewide—while Milwaukee, Waukesha, Racine, Kenosha, and Marathon Counties recorded the most cases.attomdata.com Although the rate is lower than during the Great Recession, filings have been inching up as pandemic-era protections expire.

Key takeaway: Every day you stay in the property is valuable bargaining time—use it wisely.

2. Start With Your Lender (Yes, Really)

The moment you realize you cannot make a payment, call your mortgage servicer’s loss-mitigation department. Lenders must review you for options such as:

If the servicer refuses to work with you, keep notes of every call and letter. A well-documented file strengthens later legal defenses or short-sale negotiations.

3. Tap State & Federal Relief Programs

Even though federal forbearance ended, funds are still available:

  • Wisconsin Help for Homeowners (WHH) — grants up to $40,000 for mortgage, tax, or utility arrears; nearly 8,600 households have already received an average of $8,438.content.govdelivery.com
  • Homeowner Assistance Fund (HAF) — the federal pool that finances WHH has helped over 549,000 U.S. borrowers through mid-2024.home.treasury.gov
  • WHEDA Foreclosure Prevention — state agency that offers in-house modifications for WHEDA loans and referrals to HUD-approved counselors.wheda.com

4. Get Professional Backup

Housing Counselors

HUD-certified counselors are free for foreclosure prevention and will prepare the budget package lenders require. They can also spot predatory “rescue” scams that have surged since 2023.investopedia.com

Foreclosure Attorneys

A lawyer can raise defenses (e.g., improper service, lost note) and request mediation—an option many Wisconsin borrowers overlook. Legal fees are modest compared with the long-term credit damage of a sheriff’s sale.

5. Government Programs Didn’t Pan Out? Explore Exit Strategies

  1. Refinance or reinstate if your credit and equity allow.
  2. Short sale — sell for less than the mortgage balance with lender approval. Less damaging than foreclosure but can drag on for months.
  3. Deed in lieu of foreclosure — hand the property back and walk away, but only if the lender waives any deficiency.

6. Why a Direct Cash Offer Can Be the Safest Bet

Because you choose the closing date, you can halt the foreclosure, satisfy the lender in full, and move on with a cash cushion instead of a ruined credit score.

7. Unique Insight: Don’t Fall for “Rescue” Scams

When the Lis Pendens (foreclosure notice) hits public records, scammers pounce. Red flags include:

  • Demanding up-front “consulting” fees
  • Telling you to quit-claim the deed but stay and pay rent
  • Promising to repair credit “overnight”

Wisconsin law requires anyone offering foreclosure relief to provide a written, cancelable contract. If in doubt, call the Department of Financial Institutions before signing.

8. Stay Organized to Stay in Control

Create a single binder (or cloud folder) with:

  • Court documents and deadlines
  • All correspondence with the servicer (certified-mail receipts are gold)
  • Budget worksheets and proof of income for modifications
  • Comparable sales or cash-offer estimates if you plan to sell

Being able to hand a complete packet to a counselor, lawyer, or buyer can shave weeks off the timeline.

What To Do To Stop The Foreclosure Process

Stopping the foreclosure process in Wisconsin starts with quick action:

  1. Call your lender and request loss-mitigation.
  2. Apply for WHH or other relief if you qualify.
  3. Consult a HUD counselor or attorney for guidance.
  4. Decide on your exit—and if speed and certainty matter most, call Kustom Property Solutions today. We will make a fair, no-obligation cash offer, cover standard closing costs, and let you pick the day you hand over the keys. From the first missed payment to sheriff’s sale confirmation, the average timeline is 9–15 months, depending on court backlog and the redemption period set by the judge.docs.legis.wisconsin.govdocs.legis.wisconsin.gov

2. Can I still save my home after the sheriff’s auction is scheduled?
Yes. You retain redemption rights until the court confirms the sale—typically 8–12 months after judgment—or a shorter statutory period for abandoned properties. Paying the full balance or closing a sale before confirmation will stop the process.docs.legis.wisconsin.gov

3. What is the difference between forbearance and loan modification?
Forbearance pauses or reduces payments temporarily; a modification permanently restructures your loan (rate, term, or balance) to lower monthly costs.

4. Will a short sale hurt my credit as much as foreclosure?
A short sale usually drops your credit score 50–120 points versus 150 points or more for foreclosure. Lenders and future landlords also view a completed sale more favorably.

How To Avoid Probate Court In Wisconsin

November 5, 2024

By nategifford

Nobody wants to have to go through the probate process, especially if they plan to sell the inherited property once their loved ones have passed. Dealing with the probate process can seem overwhelming. In our latest guide, discover how to avoid probate court in Wisconsin and learn simple steps you can take now to protect your family and your property.

Whether you plan to keep the inherited property or sell it after a relative passes away, it’s important to plan ahead. By being proactive, you can help your loved ones avoid lengthy court proceedings and expensive fees. In turn, your family can focus on healing and moving forward rather than getting bogged down in legalities.

Why Avoid Probate?

There are many reasons people aim to avoid probate in Wisconsin. For starters, probate can quickly become costly, with attorney charges, executor fees, and court costs piling up. While some executors may waive their fees to keep the peace within the family, other charges cannot be skipped. Beyond the expenses, probate also demands a lot of time. Assets must be officially accounted for, and proper notices must be sent to heirs. Before any inheritance is distributed to beneficiaries, all debts of the estate must be settled. This process can feel drawn out, adding stress to an already difficult period.

Another factor is privacy. Probate records can be public, meaning personal details about your loved one’s estate could become available for anyone to see. By planning to bypass probate, you can protect your family’s financial information and maintain a greater degree of confidentiality. Ultimately, avoid probate in Wisconsin if you want to spare your family lengthy paperwork, protect their privacy, and help them save on unwanted legal fees.

Using A Trust

One straightforward way to keep your assets out of probate is by setting up a trust. Specifically, a revocable living trust can give you the power to decide exactly which assets are included and how they will be handled once you are gone. Imagine a trust like a basket (or a bucket) into which you place different items, such as real estate, stocks, or personal valuables. By transferring ownership of these assets to the trust while you are still capable of making decisions, you ensure they are not subject to probate once you pass away.

It’s crucial to establish the trust at a time when you are of sound mind. This approach allows you to make thoughtful choices about who should benefit from your estate. Plus, because assets in a living trust skip probate, your heirs can inherit faster and with fewer complications. Working with a financial expert can help you structure your trust to fit your unique needs, especially if your estate holds a variety of property types.

Joint Ownership

Joint ownership is another helpful method for families trying to avoid probate court in Wisconsin. When two or more people buy property together, they can set it up as joint tenancy with the right of survivorship. This arrangement means that if one owner passes away, the other automatically becomes the sole owner of the property. No probate is required for that transfer.

While this strategy is useful, it must be arranged when you purchase the property. Adding someone to the deed after the fact can require added paperwork and fees. If you know you want the property to pass smoothly to another owner, be sure to plan the arrangement at the time of purchase. A little forethought can spare your heirs from dealing with the court system and help them hold onto the property without major legal hurdles.

Beneficiary Designations

Certain financial accounts and insurance policies allow you to name a beneficiary. For instance, bank accounts and life insurance often include a space to list who should receive the funds if you pass away. By filling out this information—and keeping it up to date—you can make sure these assets are transferred directly to the designated beneficiary. This avoids the court altogether.

In some areas, you may also create what’s known as a transfer-on-death (TOD) deed or certificate for real estate. This legal document ensures the property will instantly pass to a named individual when you die. To prevent surprises or misunderstandings, regularly review your beneficiary choices—especially after significant life changes such as divorce, remarriage, or the passing of a loved one. Neglecting updates can lead to unintended heirs or force property into the probate process, which defeats the goal of a swift, worry-free transfer.

Giving Inheritance Away

Another way to reduce what goes through the probate process is to give away part of your estate before you pass. Items that no longer belong to you do not need to be probated. The federal gift tax laws allow people to give a certain amount each year without tax penalties—often around $11,000 or so per person annually, though this figure can change. Spreading out gifts over a few years may significantly reduce the size of your estate that remains at your death.

This strategy requires planning and communication. You want to ensure the gifts you give are both meaningful and practical. Giving away large items in advance means loved ones can enjoy them sooner, and your estate shrinks in a legal sense, making the probate process either simpler or unnecessary.

Avoiding Probate for Smaller Estates

Not every estate is large or complicated. In some states, if the estate is valued under a certain threshold, the probate process can be sped up or bypassed through simpler legal forms. This threshold varies by location, so check local laws in Wisconsin to see if a small-estate procedure might apply.

These simplified processes often require filling out a special affidavit or a short form to claim assets. While this shortcut can save time and money, it’s only available if your estate’s total value is under the designated limit. If you’re uncertain about the rules in your area, consider speaking with a local professional who knows exactly what is required to finalize an estate without unnecessary court steps.

Planning Now for Peace of Mind

Ultimately, making arrangements to avoid probate in Wisconsin can save your family from hassles and stress after you’re gone. From setting up a trust to adding beneficiaries to your accounts, these small actions can have a big impact. Whether you own a single-family home or multiple investment properties, there are ways to organize your assets so your wishes are honored with the least amount of red tape.

If you have questions or want personalized guidance about how to avoid probate in Wisconsin, reach out to our team. We understand that this topic can be both legally and emotionally challenging, and we’re here to help you find the best solution for your situation.
